title: Bright or Close? Luminosity
objective: After this level you can explain the difference between how bright a star looks and how bright it really is.
summary: A star’s apparent brightness depends on its luminosity and its distance, fading with the square of distance.

cards.headline: The brightest star in the sky has a secret: it lives nearby.
cards.body: Sirius outshines every other star in the night sky. But a star can look bright for two very different reasons, and Sirius has help from the easier one.

cards.headline: Two kinds of bright
cards.body: A porch light next door can outshine a stadium floodlight across town. Stars play the same trick on you. How bright a star looks from Earth depends on two things: how much light it actually gives off, called its luminosity, and how far away it is. So a star that looks bright might be truly powerful, or just close.

mascot.line: Keep this: looking bright and being luminous are different things. Distance sits in between.

cards.headline: Fading with distance
cards.body: Distance dims starlight fast. A star’s apparent brightness falls with the square of its distance: move a star twice as far away and it looks only a quarter as bright. Ten times as far? A hundredth. If that rule sounds familiar, it should: gravity in Level 27 weakens with the square of distance too. The universe likes this pattern.
cards.callout: Twice as far → ¼ as bright

cards.fact: Sirius, the brightest night-time star, is about 8.6 light-years away.
cards.context: Sirius really is more luminous than the Sun, and it’s also relatively close. Power plus proximity: that’s the winning combination. A star with more power but far more distance can easily lose the contest.

cards.headline: Starlight: weighed
learned: Apparent brightness depends on luminosity and distance
Brightness falls with the square of distance
Sirius looks brightest partly because it’s close
Luminosity is a star’s true output

options.label: How bright it looks from Earth
How much light it actually gives off
How far away it is in light-years
How hot its surface is in degrees
options.rationale: Temperature is related, but luminosity is total output.

questions.explanation: Luminosity is a star’s true light output, regardless of distance.

questions.prompt: Match each with what it means for a star's light.

pairs.right: How much light it actually gives off

questions.explanation: Brightness falls with the square of distance: twice as far looks a quarter as bright, ten times as far a hundredth. Luminosity is how much light a star actually gives off.

questions.prompt: Which other effect weakens with the square of distance, just like starlight?

options.label: The speed of light
options.rationale: Light’s speed doesn’t change with distance.

options.label: How fast a planet spins on its axis
options.rationale: Spin rate doesn’t depend on distance from anything.

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity and starlight both spread out and weaken with the square of the distance.
